summary: Describes how to connect separate Fibre Channel storage networks over an ordinary IP network by tunneling Fibre Channel frames over TCP. This makes remote storage islands behave like one storage network, relying on IP for the connection between sites.

eli5.summary: Two storage rooms in faraway cities have their own special hallways. This document describes a tunnel through the regular road network so they act like one big building.

questions: connecting storage area networks over ip
how are fibre channel frames carried over tcp
subtitle: How to stretch a Fibre Channel storage network across an IP network by carrying its frames inside TCP connections.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel storage networks (SANs) are limited in how far apart their switches can sit, yet sites that are far apart want remote disk access, tape backup and live mirroring.
tldr.mechanism: FCIP wraps each Fibre Channel frame in an encapsulation header and sends it through one or more TCP connections between FCIP Entities, so the IP network acts like a long cable between two parts of one Fibre Channel fabric.
tldr.outcome: The two storage islands form a single Fibre Channel fabric whose devices are unaware of the IP network. RFC 3821 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7146.

facts.label: Valid Frame Length
facts.value: Greater than 15 and less than 545 words

today: RFC 3821 is a Proposed Standard from July 2004 and is updated by RFC 7146. It has not been obsoleted. Readers should consult RFC 7146 alongside it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
Fibre Channel (FC) is a gigabit or multi-gigabit networking technology used mainly for storage area networks (SANs). The RFC describes how to join separate FC SANs, called islands, over an IP network so that they form one unified SAN in a single FC fabric. The stated motivations are remote disk access, tape backup and live mirroring between physically distant sites.

The key assumption is that the FC fabric and every device on it must be unaware of the IP network. FC frames therefore have to arrive in time to meet existing Fibre Channel specifications. The RFC covers only the TCP/IP side; the Fibre Channel side is left to the T11 documents such as FC-BB-2. It does not try to replace the Fibre Channel Arbitrated Loop, and it defines no way to carry loop primitive signals.
sections.eli5: Imagine two toy towns that each have their own train tracks. FCIP lets the trains cross between the towns over the normal road, and the trains never notice.

sections.title: The FCIP Model
sections.content:
The basic unit of service is the FCIP Link. It joins two parts of an FC fabric using the IP network and contains at least one TCP connection (it MAY contain more). At each end, an FC Entity (the Fibre Channel side) is paired with an FCIP Entity (the IP side). The interface between the two is implementation specific, and the RFC lists what it requires of the FC Entity in an appendix.

Inside an FCIP Entity, an FCIP Control and Services Module handles link set-up and teardown. Each FCIP Link Endpoint (FCIP_LEP) represents one link and holds one FCIP Data Engine (FCIP_DE) for every TCP connection in that link. The Data Engine has an encapsulation engine and a de-encapsulation engine, with four portals where frames enter and leave.

Seen from the IP network, FCIP Entities are peers talking TCP/IP. Seen from the fabric, the paired entities simply forward FC frames. Primitive signals, primitive sequences and Class 1 frames are not carried, because they cannot be encoded with FC Frame Encapsulation. Routing of the encapsulated frames follows normal IP routing.
sections.eli5: At each end of the tunnel there is a gatekeeper who wraps every parcel in a plain brown box, sends it down the road, and unwraps it at the other end.

sections.title: Encapsulated Frames and the Special Frame
sections.content:
Every FC frame is carried in an FCIP Frame: the FC frame plus the encapsulation header from RFC 3643, with an encoded start-of-frame (SOF) and end-of-frame (EOF). In the header, the Protocol# field is 1 for FCIP. The protocol-specific pFlags field has two defined bits: SF (Special Frame) and Ch (Changed). The CRC valid flag and the CRC field are set to 0.

The FCIP Special Frame (FSF) is a specially formatted frame with SF set to 1. It is sent only as the first bytes in each direction on a new TCP connection, and only one is sent each way. Among its fields are the source FC Fabric Entity World Wide Name, a source FC/FCIP Entity Identifier, a 64-bit random Connection Nonce, connection usage flags and code, the destination World Wide Name, and the K_A_TOV keep-alive timeout.

The FSF does three jobs: it identifies the link endpoints, it conveys a few critical parameters, and, where site security policy allows, it can be used for simple configuration discovery. The RFC stresses that it is not a login or parameter negotiation mechanism.
sections.eli5: The first note passed through a new tunnel is a name tag that says who is sending and who they think is receiving. After that, only ordinary parcels travel.

sections.title: Error Detection and Resynchronization
sections.content:
FCIP leans on TCP for in-order delivery and checksums, so the byte stream reaching the Data Engine is already ordered and free of errors TCP can detect. The Data Engine still checks that the stream is correctly delimited and that the Protocol# and version fields hold the values defined for FCIP.

The Frame Length field tells the receiver where the next header starts. Synchronization is considered lost if the length is not greater than 15 and less than 545 (in words), if the length does not match its ones complement, or if the word before the next header does not hold a valid EOF with its complement. The RFC explains the lower bound: seven header words, one each for the encoded SOF and EOF, six for the FC header and one for the FC CRC give a base of 16 words, and the maximum FC payload is 528 words.

Beyond those tests, the RFC lists 16 further checks on the encapsulation, and at least 3 of the 16 SHALL be performed. A frame failing any test that is run is not forwarded to the FC Entity. If the Data Engine cannot find the next header, it closes the TCP connection, or searches for a valid header and discards bytes until it finds one, or tries the search first and closes the connection if that fails. Recovery from discarded data is left to the FC Entity and the rest of the fabric. Appendix D gives an example resynchronization algorithm.
sections.eli5: Every parcel says how long it is, so the receiver knows where the next one starts. If the receiver loses count, it either hangs up or scans forward until it spots a proper parcel label again.

sections.title: Opening TCP Connections
sections.content:
An FCIP Entity must know the peer's IP address and port before connecting, either by configuration or by dynamic discovery. Dynamic discovery SHALL use the Service Location Protocol version 2 as defined for FCIP in RFC 3822. The connect request goes to the FCIP well-known port, 3225, unless another port is configured. If a request is rejected, the entity SHALL avoid hammering the peer; the RFC suggests waiting 60 seconds as an example.

Once the connection is accepted, the initiator sends an FSF and keeps a copy. The receiver checks the nonce and the destination World Wide Name and, if all is acceptable, echoes the FSF unchanged. The initiator compares the echo with what it sent (words 7 through 17) and closes the connection if they differ. Timeouts of not less than 90 seconds MAY be used while waiting. Only after a successful echo does the entity apply quality of service settings, create the link endpoint if needed, create a Data Engine and tell the FC Entity.

A receiver may alter the FSF, for example to fill in its own World Wide Name when the sender put zero there. It then sets the Ch bit, echoes the changed frame and closes the connection. The sender learns the peer's identity this way and a later attempt will probably succeed. If a new connection claims the same source identity as an existing link, the FC Entity must authenticate it before the connection is used.

The RFC also gives TCP advice: an FCIP Entity MAY use selective acknowledgement, window scaling should match the local buffers and the bandwidth-delay product, protection against wrapped sequence numbers (PAWS) is RECOMMENDED, and the Nagle algorithm should be disabled. Flow control in Fibre Channel is credit based while TCP is window based; coordinating the two is declared outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.eli5: When a new tunnel lane opens, one side shows its name tag and the other side repeats it back exactly. If the tag comes back wrong, they hang up and try again later.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Replacing a protected cable with an IP network exposes the fabric to attacks it did not face before: the RFC says a fabric is only as secure as the IP network carrying its FCIP links. Listed threats include monitoring or altering traffic, hijacking TCP connections, injecting frames, masquerading as an FCIP Entity, denial of service through connection requests, attacks on discovery, and replaying the observed contents of an FSF. The TCP checksum, the FCIP ones complement checks and the FC frame CRC do not stop a determined attacker, since all can be regenerated.

FCIP therefore requires IPsec. Implementations MUST support ESP in tunnel mode, with per-packet origin authentication, integrity and replay protection, and ESP with NULL encryption if confidentiality is off. They MUST implement HMAC with SHA-1 and 3DES in CBC mode, and SHOULD implement AES. DES in CBC mode SHOULD NOT be used. Keys come from IKE; manual keying SHALL NOT be used, pre-shared keys MUST be supported, and certificates MAY be. The default SA lifetime is one hour and the default anti-replay window is 32 sequence numbers.

Each TCP connection MUST be protected by an IKE Phase 2 SA. On an integrity failure the receiver MUST drop the datagram, which triggers a TCP retransmission, and it MAY close the connection if this happens often.
sections.eli5: A tunnel through public roads needs locks. FCIP says every parcel must be sealed and checked so nobody can peek inside or slip in a fake one.

sections.title: Performance and Quality of Service
sections.content:
Links inside an FC fabric are normally low latency and high throughput, and an IP network is less certain on both counts. The RFC allows several TCP connections within one link so that different traffic can get different treatment. When a connection is created, the FC Entity specifies its quality of service (QoS) characteristics, and they SHALL NOT change for the life of that connection.

It is RECOMMENDED that some form of preferential QoS be used to reduce latency and packet drops, though no particular form is mandated. Any per-hop behavior implemented is RECOMMENDED to interoperate with diffserv. If no preferential QoS is used, the DSCP field SHOULD be set to 000000. For networks with a large bandwidth-delay product, window scaling and protection against wrapped sequence numbers are RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: A long tunnel can be slow, so FCIP lets you put important parcels in a fast lane and pick the lane when the tunnel opens.
